While I am constrained by time to perform all of this work, I hope that we can explore some ways that a system could be built to accomplish this. I'm thinking of using JavaScript and HTML to be able to create a visual system. Working with Excalibur would, of course, work as well. So would Obsidian. And of course, so would an Ebsidian Excalibur plugin. Attached 1 file. - Sketch-Your-Mind.pdf
turns.response_html:
Translating books into a 4D, spatial format using Zsolt Viczián's "Sketch-Your-Mind" methodology is a brilliant approach to personal knowledge management. Moving from flat, linear text to interconnected visual "LEGO blocks" allows you to navigate concepts rather than just read them.

Since time is a constraint, trying to manually sketch and map every insight from a library of books isn't feasible. But you can architect a highly automated, local-first system to do the heavy lifting. By leveraging the Obsidian Excalidraw plugin’s scripting engine alongside your own automation pipelines, you can programmatically generate these visual hybrid notes.

Here is a blueprint for building an automated 4D visual thinking system.

1. The Engine: Local Agents and Data Extraction

Before drawing anything, you need to break the books down into modular concepts. Instead of manually highlighting and summarizing, you can deploy a local agentic framework to process the text.

  • Parsing: Feed the book's text into a local LLM.
  • Extraction: Prompt the agent to identify core concepts, metaphors, and relationships, adhering to the "Card Forcing Function" (distilling ideas into a single title, 3 key points, and a suggested visual symbol).
  • Formatting: Have the agent output this data as structured JSON.

2. The Bridge: Obsidian Excalidraw Automate API

The Obsidian Excalidraw plugin has a powerful API called ExcalidrawAutomate. You can write JavaScript (often executed via the Templater plugin) to consume your agent's JSON and procedurally generate the drawings.

Example Workflow: You can write a script that instantiates the API (const ea = ExcalidrawAutomate; ea.reset();), reads the JSON output, and uses functions like ea.addText() and ea.addArrow() to lay out the nodes. You can even fetch predefined icons from your local curated library to match the extracted concepts.

3. The Architecture: Structuring the 4D Space

To keep this automated system organized and prevent your vault from turning into a chaotic web, route the generated visual outputs into distinct cognitive realms.

  • Map: Direct the highest-level architectural overviews of the books here. Use the API to automatically generate an "Idea Atlas" or a "Concept Map" that shows how the book's chapters and primary arguments connect.
  • Garden: Send the atomic, modular concepts here. These are your generated Hybrid Notes (a visual front with structured text on the back). Over time, these evergreen visual Zettels will cross-pollinate as different books share similar nodes.
  • Lab: Dedicate this space to your "Idea Integration Boards" and "Double-Bubble Maps." You can write scripts that take two seemingly unrelated concepts from your system and automatically chart them side-by-side to test for hidden tension or serendipitous connections.
  • Planet: For the final, polished output, use Excalidraw's export features (ea.createSVG() or ea.createPNG()). You can bundle these visuals into a lightweight, decentralized HTML/JavaScript front-end to share your insights outside of your local environment.

4. The Workflow: Terminal-Centric Execution

You can tie all of this together without leaving your preferred environment.

  • Triggering: Write a Fish shell script that takes a raw text file or an epub, passes it to your local LLM for extraction, and saves the JSON into your vault.
  • Execution: Use Neovim to quickly review or tweak the JSON data.
  • Rendering: Trigger the Obsidian URI scheme from your terminal to execute the Excalidraw template, instantly rendering the JSON into a 4D spatial map.

Building this pipeline requires some upfront engineering, but once the agentic parsing and ExcalidrawAutomate scripts are locked in, turning a dense book into a navigable visual landscape becomes a background process.

Which part of the automation pipeline—the LLM entity extraction or the Excalidraw JavaScript rendering—would you like to tackle first?

The Invariant Compiler Pipeline

Process 1: Structural Parsing & Macro-Orientation (Structural Reading)

Before analyzing a single sentence, the compiler must map the geometry of the text. This process establishes the master boundaries of the knowledge domain.

  • The Invariant Operation: The system extracts the Table of Contents, Preface, and Introduction to build a high-level topographical map.
  • The Compiler's Stance: It identifies the author's primary system of thought—their "Idea Atlas" skeleton—before processing individual chapters. This prevents downstream extraction from becoming a chaotic pool of unlinked nodes.

Process 2: Concept Distillation via the Forcing Function (Atomic Chunking)

The compiler must break long paragraphs into distinct, modular units of meaning.

  • The Invariant Operation: Every block of extracted text must pass through a strict spatial constraint: the Card Forcing Function. . It must compress the insight into a single sharp title, exactly 3 key points, and a single core metaphor or symbol. If an extraction fails this layout constraint, it is iteratively broken down into smaller child nodes until it fits.

Process 3: Functional Categorization & Ontology Mapping (LATCH Tagging)

To turn data into a navigable terrain, every extracted concept must be automatically fitted with retrieval metadata.

  • The Invariant Operation: The compiler passes every atomic card through the LATCH framework to generate indexing hooks.
  • The Compiler's Stance: The scripts must determine a concept's Category functional type (e.g., #ZK/PN for permanent notes, #quote, #concept), its Time anchor (sequence in the book or when it was processed), and its Hierarchy scale (whether it's a broad parent concept or a detailed child node).

. The compiler must actively force new extractions to interface with existing nodes.

  • The Invariant Operation: The extraction engine applies the Idea Compass to every new card, questioning its place in the wider web of thought.
  • The Compiler's Stance: The agent evaluates the extraction in four fixed axes:
    • North (Parents): What foundational concept or historical origin does this build on?
    • South (Children): What downstream application or detailed consequence does this lead to?
    • West (Friends): What similar models or supporting arguments echo this note?
    • East (Competitors): What idea contradicts, challenges, or limits this stance?

Process 5: Narrative Synthesis & Tension Resolution (South Park "Glue")

A compiler cannot just dump structural components; it must assemble them into a meaningful delivery system—a single-page story map.

  • The Invariant Operation: The system takes the distilled concepts and applies causal narrative logic to determine their sequence.
  • The Compiler's Stance: It strips out passive "and then" ordering. It forces the extraction to map out causal dependencies using "but" and "therefore" transitions. .

Implementing the Scripting Strategies

To make this invariant compiler system real, we can design different analyzer scripts to attack the PDF text depending on its structural complexity:

  1. The Structural Scraping Script: Excellent for highly structured books (textbooks, technical manuals). It uses programmatic regex or markdown hierarchies to auto-map Process 1 and Process 3 straight from the index and H1/H2 tags.
  2. The Semantic Windowing Script: Ideal for fluid, dense prose (philosophy, essays). It slides an overlapping token window across the text, using local embedding comparisons to look for semantic shifts, flagging where a concept changes so Process 2 can kick in and force a new card synthesis.
  3. The Agentic Dialectic Script: Perfect for books with conflicting viewpoints. It sets up two local LLM instances—one acts as the Champion of the author's stance, the other acts as the Challenger. As the book text streams in, their debate automatically Populates the West (Friends) and East (Competitors) fields of the Idea Compass.

Another thing. We could visualize with some kind of heat map or point cloud or graph of some sort the density of information through the text. So that then, when we actually compile it, we can compare the density visuals to see what we smooth over.
turns.response_html:
This is a critical architectural step. If your compiler is translating linear text into a spatial, 4D visual system, that translation is inherently a form of data compression.

To measure what gets "smoothed over" or lost in translation, you need a baseline. By grading the raw text's information density before extraction, you create a structural topology of the book. Later, you can overlay the density of your generated visual nodes against this original topology to spot the gaps.

Here are three programmatic heuristics you can use to grade the text's "richness":

1. Entity Saturation (The Node Count)

This measures the pure volume of distinct concepts.

  • The Heuristic: Run a Named Entity Recognition (NER) pass or a keyword extraction algorithm over a rolling window (e.g., every 500 words).
  • The Metric: A high ratio of unique, domain-specific nouns to common filler words indicates a dense cluster of ideas.

2. Causal Velocity (The Edge Density)

Information isn't just about nouns; it's about how they interact. A text might have few entities but highly complex arguments linking them.

  • The Heuristic: Measure the frequency of logical operators and transition friction—words like therefore, however, because, implies, contradicts.
  • The Metric: Spikes in causal velocity indicate dense argumentative logic (the "South Park Glue"), whereas drops indicate narrative filler, anecdotes, or examples.

3. Lexical Entropy (The Signal-to-Noise Ratio)

Borrowing from signal processing, this grades the unpredictability of the text.

  • The Heuristic: Calculate the semantic variance of the embeddings in a given paragraph. If a paragraph repeats the same concept in five different ways, its entropy is low. If every sentence introduces a wildly different vector, the entropy is high.
  • The Metric: High entropy areas are "high-risk" zones for your compiler—these are the dense, rapid-fire sections where your scripts are most likely to drop crucial context if they chunk too broadly.

Visualizing the Topology

By plotting these metrics along the X-axis (the progression of the book), you generate an "Information Heatmap" or a continuous point cloud. When your compiler finishes generating the visual map, you run the exact same heuristics on the generated JSON output. If the original text had a massive spike in Causal Velocity in Chapter 4, but your extracted visual map for Chapter 4 is sparse, you immediately know your extraction script smoothed over critical data.
